title: Breaking and Entering: Acopia on Friendship, Transience, and the Things Left Unsaid
transcript:
Kate Durman and Morgan Wright of Acopia joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studios ahead of the band's sold-out show at the Night Cat. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 18 June 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: I'm joined in the RRR studios by two members of the local trio Acopia, Kate Durman and Morgan Wright. Thanks for joining me.

Kate: It's a pleasure to be here. Thanks for having us.

Lauren: We should mention the other member of your trio, Lachlan, who's unfortunately unwell and unable to join us today. Your show at the Night Cat has sold out, so you're not here with anything to promote, just having a chat. And you've been up to quite a bit: some big tours, and making really great waves overseas. You got back from a couple of months away in North America, the UK and Europe. Is it nice to be back in your hometown for a bit?

Kate: It is. I personally really miss the food a lot. Most of all — oh, most of all my friends, probably. But the produce and food was a close second. Not to be ungrateful. It was an amazing tour, and a really positive experience. So grateful to have gone there.

Lauren: Do you have first places you go to when you tour overseas, to orient yourself in a new city? I know lots of people like to start at record stores.

Morgan: Probably just a good pub meal or something. Or Pret, in Europe or the UK. So good.

Kate: We should do that, though. That's actually wise. That sounds way smarter.

Lauren: How do the members of Acopia go touring together? Is it all pretty smooth sailing?

Morgan: It's pretty good. Now we've done a few international tours and have spent a lot of time around each other, in each other's pockets, I would say by now we can read each other very well. For instance, noticing when we need to give each other a bit of space.

Kate: Yeah, definitely. We all need quite a bit of space, so we get to have a lot of downtime and do our own thing. But we always go and eat dinners and stuff together, which is really nice.

Lauren: You've described working with Acopia as a surreal experience, writing music with your best friends. What is it about writing together that feels so surreal or unique?

Kate: I'll let you answer that, Morgan. That's for you.

Morgan: Thank you, Kate. I think primarily the fact that it's really fun and actually enjoyable. Sometimes collaborating can be a bit of a slog. But what makes it really easy for the project is that all of us can play instruments and produce. So if we want to communicate an idea, we can do words, but then you can also just show each other the idea.

Lauren: Looking back over the three albums you've done together now, does your personal history and friendship shape the sound of Acopia in a way you might not have anticipated?

Morgan: Well, like I was saying, we spend a lot of time together, in a positive way, by the way, and our friendship with each other is all very strong because of that. It might not have been as strong if we weren't doing this project together.

Lauren: In terms of the sound, though.

Morgan: I think, yeah, definitely. I feel like whenever we make music, we always spend probably a quarter of the time debriefing emotionally about stuff that's stressing us out, but also talking about just everything happening in the world. As humans we're going to be affected by everything around us, and that's going to impact our craft. As the albums have gone along, you can communicate that maybe a bit clearer, or we're all maybe better at channelling a certain emotion, or trying to elicit a certain emotion in the listener through the songwriting or the production. I feel like we're much better at that now.

Lauren: All three of you are accomplished electronic producers in your own right, with projects outside Acopia: Kate with Purient, who we heard from a bit earlier in the show; Lachlan as one half of Tambo's House with River Yarra; and Morgan, you're releasing music under your own name. You've said Acopia was born from a shared curiosity in the genre's softer, ethereal corners, outside the club space. What drew you to that side of the music, and how did that shared interest evolve into the creative vision behind the band?

Kate: Initially we all just really wanted to collaborate together. And because of our own projects being in the dance music world, we were kind of set on, or fixated even on, having slower songs, like 80, 90, 100 BPM. I think that naturally had us gravitating, especially on the first record, towards elements of trip-hop and slowed-down breakbeats, because we'd all been producing faster music with breakbeats. And we all have a strong affection for some of the same bands, in particular Radio Dept.

So as the records have been written and evolved, we've started to learn more about one another's music tastes on the softer side, rather than just sharing club tracks or whatever. And then COVID happened, maybe a year after the band had started, and I think that changed the songs we wrote as well, leaning into that more home-listening, chilled-out sound.

Lauren: You were talking before about emotions. Are there specific emotions or environments you're trying to evoke through Acopia when you step away from that traditional late-night energy?

Kate: I guess it's just going inwards a bit more, as a whole, as a concept even. And like you were saying, Morgan, about how we debrief a lot of the time before we go into writing something, I think it's helped us become more open people. So maybe, yeah, maybe that. Did that make sense? I hope so. I've forgotten the question now. What was the question?

Morgan: Me too.

Lauren: No, you answered it very well. Some people have identified a really dreamlike quality in your music, and you mentioned going inward. Are dreams an important source of information or inspiration for Acopia at all?

Morgan: I feel like maybe thematically sometimes: fragmented bits of dreams, or ideas, or feelings. There's been a couple of times where I, or one of us, has had a dream about a song or an idea, and we've worked on it. Can't say it has been good, but we've done it before.

Kate: Yeah. I think my dreams relating to Acopia are all just airport-related stress dreams, like forgetting my passport.

Lauren: Your album title, Blush Response, which was a Triple R album of the week last year, references the phrase from Blade Runner: it's used in a test to distinguish humans from replicants, measuring their emotional reactions. What drew you to that concept, and how does the title connect to the themes or emotions you're exploring on the record?

Morgan: I'll let you handle that one, Kate. You came up with the idea.

Kate: I was re-watching the original Blade Runner, and it's one of the phrases they use quite early on. I just thought it was a cool concept, because it's trying to work out if something is — what was the word? Not robot, a replicant, whatever that means. I just thought about it as an emotional thing, like maybe some people that have difficulty with connecting to certain emotions, and needing to kind of sit with it for a bit to work out what they're really feeling or experiencing. And it's something that I've experienced before. I just thought it kind of sounded like what the album sounds like, in a way.

Lauren: You've also talked about blushing itself being a really raw and involuntary thing, a true reminder that you're alive: the exact moment an internal feeling becomes an external reaction. What was it about that idea that resonated so strongly?

Kate: It's just really cute. Blushing is really cute, and having a crush on someone's really cute, and it makes you feel alive. And a lot of our songs are love songs, or kind of about breakups, or learning who you are and what you're about. So I think it's just that, really.

Lauren: 'Talk About It', you've said, explores fears of emotional intimacy and the piling weight of all things left unspoken. Can you share a bit more about that track, and why you were drawn to exploring it?

Kate: I think at the time I — oh, wait, maybe it was Lachie at the time. I hope he won't mind me saying this. We were in the room starting to write this idea, and he was in a bit of a funk, and we're like, "What's going on?" And he said, "I don't want to talk about it." And I was like, boom. Write that down. Someone write that down.

Lauren: That's it. The location for the recording sounds really interesting as well. You've described it as looking like a nineties movie set of a washed-up office building in South Yarra, and the building itself was set for demolition.

Morgan: It's not there anymore. You can't even go there.

Lauren: Did knowing that the space would soon be gone influence your mindset during those recording sessions?

Kate: I think so, because it's weird to go into a space when you know it's not going to be there anymore. It's kind of like when you think about time and how short it is, not to get on that level, but yeah, it was cool. The days were numbered there, so we had to just be in it.

Morgan: And the aura was kind of threatening in there. If all the lights were on, fluorescent white lights, there were still computers, old computers. It was very weird, but cool energy.

Kate: Yeah. Threatening, but cool. It's gone now.

Lauren: So do you think that sense of transience makes its way onto the record?

Morgan: Yeah, I think so. That's a good word. I like that one.

Lauren: A very big thank you to Morgan and Kate from Acopia for dropping by and having a chat with me. The record is Blush Response.
